docs.text: Item Cost ($) Item Cost ($) Phone 300 Flashlight 20 Handcuffs 30 Multitool 40 Burner phone 20 Radio, pair 80 Zip ties (UD8) 5 Duct tape (UD6) 5 Laptop 800 First aid kit (UD6) 50 Rope, 50 ft 20 Fuel can (UD8) 30 Camera 400 Painkillers (UD6) 20 Crowbar 20 Camera, hidden 300 Voice recorder 50 Body bag 30 Bolt cutters 40 Fake ID 500 Binoculars 100 Notebook (UD6) 20 Lockpicks 100 Pens (UD8) 5

docs.title: Vehicles
docs.text:
Vehicle Cost ($) Notes Car 8000 Distant in one round on open road. Four passengers Motorcycle 4000 Two passengers. Advantage on Driving in traffic Van 12000 Slow. 60 slots of cargo, or six people Boat, small 15000

Light: a flashlight is near range and a phone screen is close range. Both run on a UD8 rolled each hour. Everything in Section 6's Light rules otherwise applies — a modern game is not as well-lit as people assume once the power's out.

docs.title: A5. Optional Rules
docs.text:
Lethal firearms. The list above keeps guns level with medieval weapons, which suits pulp and horror. For a game where a gunshot is a catastrophe, shift every firearm up one die and give non-ballistic armour no AC against them. Apply it to the enemies too — that's the whole point, and it makes a single hallway genuinely frightening.

Response time. Modern settings have police, ambulances, and fire crews. When something loud happens, roll a d6: that's how many rounds until sirens are audible. This one die does more to shape modern play than any equipment rule.

Paper trails. Everything modern characters do leaves a record — cameras, card transactions, phone location. Rather than tracking it, give the GM one Trace token each time the party is careless. Spent later, a Trace means someone found them.

docs.title: The information problem
docs.text:
This is the appendix's central difficulty and it needs solving at your table before session one.

Fantasy runs on a small information horizon: past a day's walk, everything is rumour, so the GM invents it and no one can check. Modern characters have a phone. Any mystery you improvise can be dissolved by a player who says "I look it up."

Don't ban the phone. Answer it. Pick whichever fits:

  • No signal. Basements, tunnels, storms, rural dead zones, deliberate jamming. Cheap, effective, and a reason to keep moving.
  • The record is wrong. The information exists and it's false — the file was altered, the obituary was printed for someone still alive. Now the search is the clue.
  • Access, not knowledge. They know the file exists. Getting it means a warrant, a favour, or a break-in. The obstacle moves from knowing to reaching.
  • It isn't written down. The thing they're chasing predates records, or is deliberately absent from them. A search that returns nothing is itself information.

The last one is the best of the four, and it's why modern horror works: the terrifying result is the empty one.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Modern Rath is not action-hero fiction by default. Characters have the same 10 + CON hit points as everyone else, which is two or three shots. The genre this system naturally produces is crime, investigation, and horror — people out of their depth in a world that mostly makes sense. Lean into that before you try to make it Die Hard.

Ordinary characters are the strength here. A nurse, a mechanic, and a reporter make a better party than three ex-special-forces operators, because the interesting question is what they're willing to do, not what they're able to.

And the world is documented, populated, and legible in a way a fantasy world isn't — which cuts both ways. Your players know how a hospital works, so you don't have to explain it. They also know what should happen when someone calls 911, which means the moment nobody comes is worth ten paragraphs of description.

docs.title: 1. What is Rath RPG?
docs.text:
Rath is a rules-light fantasy roleplaying game. You play adventurers exploring dangerous places, fighting monsters, and getting into trouble. The rules stay out of your way so you can focus on what your character does, not what the rulebook allows.

The game is dangerous. Characters can die. Smart play, teamwork, and knowing when to run matter more than character builds. There are no balanced encounters—some fights are unwinnable, and that's intentional.

Characters are simple. You're defined by three things:

  • Stats — Six numbers that determine what you're good at
  • Aptitudes — Special abilities from training or innate nature
  • Inventory — What you carry, including equipped spells

Keywords tie your choices together. They're narrative descriptors (Dwarf, Fighter, Sailor) that justify advantage when relevant and help define who you are in the world.

This book is fantasy, but the rules aren't. Sections 2 through 5 don't know what century you're in — only the aptitude lists and the equipment do. Appendix A swaps those for the modern day and Appendix B for science fiction, and Section 7 covers running a game that uses more than one. Start here either way: fantasy is the setting these rules assume, and the easiest one to subtract from.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
When you attempt something uncertain with consequences, roll a test:

d20 + relevant stat ≥ DC

The default target is DC 12. Meet or beat the DC to succeed (12+ with no modifier).

  • Natural 20: Critical success — something extra good happens
  • Natural 1: Critical failure — something goes wrong

Most things in Rath use this same roll. Attack a goblin? d20 + STR vs its armor. Pick a lock? d20 + DEX vs DC 12. Convince a guard? d20 + CHA vs DC 12.

Variable Targets: The DC 12 default applies to general tests. Combat rolls target the enemy's AC instead.

docs.title: The Six Stats
docs.text:
Stat Used For STR Melee attacks, lifting, breaking, physical power DEX Ranged attacks, dodging, climbing, sneaking INT Magic, resisting magic, recalling lore, crafting WIS Perception, tracking, navigation, finding secrets CON Resisting poison/sickness, added to healing and HP CHA Persuasion, deception, intimidation, charm

Stats typically range from 0 to 3 using the standard array, or 1 to 6 if rolling. They can reach up to 10 at high levels.

docs.title: The Advantage Scale
docs.text:
Tests exist on a four-step scale:

Impossible → Disadvantage → Straight Roll → Advantage

Step How to Roll When It Applies Impossible Can't attempt No tools, no training, physically can't be done Disadvantage 2d20, take lower Poor conditions, injuries, working against your nature Straight Roll 1d20 Default for most tests Advantage 2d20, take higher Keywords apply, aptitudes help, favorable conditions

Moving on the Scale: - Keywords, aptitudes, good tools, and clever tactics move you up - Poor conditions, missing tools, and injuries move you down - Each factor moves you one step (a keyword moves you from straight to advantage, or from disadvantage to straight)

Stacking: Multiple factors in the same direction don't stack beyond one step—you can't get "double advantage." But a factor that would grant advantage can cancel out a disadvantage, moving you back to a straight roll.

Cancellation: If you have factors pushing both up and down, they cancel one-for-one. One advantage and one disadvantage = straight roll.

docs.title: Fortune Points
docs.text:
Fortune points let you push your luck. Maximum 3.

To use: After rolling any test, spend 1 Fortune to reroll and keep the higher result. You can spend Fortune on an ally's roll if you're in position to help—describe how.

Earning Fortune: - Start each session with 1 - Gain 1 when you roll a natural 20 - GM may award for heroic moments

docs.title: Understanding "L"
docs.text:
Throughout this book, "L" means your character level.

"L times per long rest" means once at level 1, twice at level 2, and so on. "Ld6 damage" means 1d6 at level 1, 2d6 at level 2, etc.

docs.title: 3. Creating a Character
docs.text:
Here's what you'll do:

  1. Choose 2 Aptitudes — Your special abilities
  2. Choose Keywords — Species, role, and optionally background
  3. Assign Stats — Distribute numbers or roll them
  4. Calculate Derived Stats — HP, AC, and inventory slots
  5. Choose Equipment — Pick a pack or roll for gear

That's it. You can be ready to play in ten minutes.

docs.title: Step 1: Choose Aptitudes
docs.text:
Choose 2 aptitudes from the list below. These define what your character can do that others can't.

Skill Aptitudes are learned abilities—anyone can take them.

Inherent Aptitudes are innate traits that define your nature.

Your aptitude choices determine your species: - 2 Skill Aptitudes = Human - 1+ Inherent Aptitudes = Demihuman (Dwarf, Elf, Halfling, Beastfolk, etc.)

Aptitude Precedence: When an aptitude contradicts a general rule in this book, the aptitude takes precedence. Specific always beats general.

Playing modern or science fiction? Use the aptitude list in Appendix A or Appendix B instead of the one below. Everything else in this section works unchanged.

docs.title: Skill Aptitudes
docs.text:
• Melee Combat
    • Cleave: Reduce enemy to 0 HP → free attack on another enemy in close range. Chain until you miss, run out of targets, or reach L attacks
    • Protect: Ally in close range hit → intercept as reaction, take the damage. With shield: CON test DC 12 for half damage
    • Resilient: +2 HP per level. Advantage vs stunned/dazed/unconscious
    • Duelist: Crit range 18-20. Advantage when fighting 1-on-1
    • Second Wind: Once per short rest, action to recover L × 1d6 HP
    • Berserker: L times/long rest, rage as free action. While raging: +1 melee damage, advantage on STR tests. Ends when combat ends or you choose
  • Ranged Combat
    • Hawkeye: Miss with bow → next attack has advantage
    • Marksman: Action to aim (give up attack) → next ranged attack has advantage + 1d6 damage
  • Assassin
    • Backstab: Attack unaware target or with advantage → dagger deals extra damage dice (1 die at L1-4, 2 dice at L5-8, 3 dice at L9-10)
    • Dagger Master: Always have a dagger. Only dagger (no shield/other weapons): +1 AC, advantage vs larger weapons once per combat
  • Exploration
    • Break and Enter: Advantage to pick locks and disable traps with thieves' tools. Complex traps/locks: roll normally. Can attempt without tools at disadvantage
    • Move Silently and Unseen: Advantage to sneak, hide, move quietly, remain undetected
    • Wild Walker: Advantage to track, hunt, forage, navigate in natural wilderness
    • Dungeon Sense: Advantage to detect traps, secret doors, unusual construction. Learn trap details when searching. Know depth and direction underground
  • Social
    • Silver Tongue: Advantage on CHA to negotiate, improve reactions, convince (not against core interests)
  • Divine
    • Heal: Once per short rest, tend creature 10 minutes → heal (L+1)d6 + WIS HP
    • Turn Undead: L times/long rest, WIS test DC 12 → undead in near range with HD ≤ 2d6 + L flee for 1d4 rounds
  • Magic
    • Hedge Magic: Minor magical tricks. INT test DC 12 to use (failure = nothing happens, no cost).
      • Candlelight: Floating light illuminates close range, lasts 1 hour
      • Spark: Ignite flammables or create small flame in palm
      • Mend: Repair small broken non-magical object (1 minute)
      • Freshen: Clean, warm, chill, or remove odors from touched object/creature
      • Trick: Minor sensory effect—small sound, puff of smoke, brief shimmer
    • Chartomancer: Cast spells from scrolls. When you cast from a scroll, make an INT test DC 12 to preserve it—success means the scroll survives, failure destroys it. Advantage if INT > scroll level, disadvantage if INT < scroll level. Casting requires both hands and can be interrupted (if hit while casting, INT test DC 12 or spell fails and scroll is destroyed). Scrolls take 1 inventory slot each. Start with one level 1 scroll of your choice.

docs.title: Inherent Aptitudes
docs.text:
These define what your character IS, not what they've learned.

  • Sensory
    • Darkvision: See near distance in pitch darkness
    • NightVision: See like daytime if any light exists (starlight counts). Not in total darkness
  • Physical
    • Natural Weapons: Claws, teeth, spines. 1d6 + STR damage
    • Natural Armor: Scales, plates, hide. +2 AC. Can't wear manufactured armor. Can use shields
    • Small: Tiny (object-sized). Advantage to hide and fit through tight spaces. Ride medium creatures. -3 inventory slots (minimum 7). Weapons deal one die size smaller (d8→d6, d6→d4, minimum d4). With Wings: true flight
    • Wings: Glide short distances, break falls. Can't fly alone. With Small: true flight
  • Combat
    • Tough: Advantage on STR tests
    • Shifty: Larger enemy misses → force them to attack another target in range (may target self)
    • Hard to Pin Down: Advantage on opposed DEX tests
    • Underfoot: Move through spaces of larger creatures. Larger enemies have disadvantage on opportunity attacks against you

docs.title: Combat
docs.text:
Initiative: Each round, all PCs roll d20 + DEX vs DC 12.

  • Success (12+): You act before monsters
  • Failure: You act after monsters

Reroll each round.

Turn order: Successful PCs → Monsters → Failed PCs

Ultra-simple variant: Roll 1d6 instead. On 1-3, enemies act first. On 4-6, players act first.

On Your Turn: - Move up to near distance + take an action (attack, cast, use item, etc.) - OR Run up to far distance (no action)

Attacking: Roll d20 + STR (melee) or DEX (ranged) vs target's AC. Meet or beat AC to hit.

Damage: Roll your weapon's damage die. Add STR to melee damage.

Exploding Damage: When you roll maximum on a damage die, roll again and add. Keep rolling if you keep hitting max.

Critical Hit (Natural 20): Target loses 1 AC until combat ends.

Fumble (Natural 1): Something goes wrong—drop weapon, slip, enemy gets advantage next attack. GM decides.

docs.title: Combat Maneuvers
docs.text:
Two Weapons: After your first attack, make a second with disadvantage.

Sacrifice Shield: Destroy your shield to absorb up to 15 damage.

docs.title: Reactions
docs.text:

docs.title: Injury and Death
docs.text:

2d6 Result 2-3 Dead — Make your final words count 4-6 Maimed — Permanent injury (GM determines). Gain 1d6 HP 7-9 Broken — Need 1 week bed rest. Gain 1d6 HP 10-11 Battered — Need 1 day rest. Gain 1d6 HP 12 Tough Bastard — Gain 2d6 HP, return to action!

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text: Hazards like poison, fire, and disease inflict conditions—ongoing effects that persist until cured or fought off. Your GM tracks condition severity and tells you when to roll saves or take damage. Common conditions include poisoned, burning, bleeding, and diseased.

docs.text:

Long Rest (6-8 hours of sleep in safe location): - Recover full HP - All abilities recharge - Can spend XP to level up

docs.title: Advancement
docs.text:
Earning XP: Gain 1 XP per session where something substantial happened.

Leveling Up: Spend XP equal to your current level during a long rest. - Level 1→2: 1 XP - Level 2→3: 2 XP - Level 3→4: 3 XP - (and so on...)

When You Level Up:

  1. Increase One Stat: +1 to any stat. No stat above 10 or above Level + 2.

  2. Gain Aptitude (at levels 3, 5, 7, 9): Choose from Basic Aptitudes or ask your GM about Advanced options. Maximum 6 aptitudes total.

  3. Roll for HP: Roll d8s equal to new level + CON. If higher than current max, that's your new max. If equal or lower, add 1 to current max.

docs.title: 7. Mixing Settings
docs.text:
This book is fantasy. The two appendices behind it are modern and science fiction, and they are not separate games — they are parts bins for this one.

Everything in Sections 2 through 5 is genre-blind. The stats, the DCs, the advantage scale, the damage and slot scales, the injury table: none of it knows or cares what century you're in. Only three things change between settings — the aptitude list, the keyword suggestions, and the equipment. That's what the appendices hold, and it's why you can take from them freely without converting anything.

How to do it: decide what your game is about, then pull the pieces that serve it. Tell your players which appendices are on the table before character creation. That's the whole procedure.

docs.title: Fantasy is the default for a reason
docs.text:
It isn't tradition. It's that fantasy characters have a small information horizon — everything past a day's walk is rumour, so the GM can invent it at the table and no one can check. That's what makes improvised play work, and it's the thing the other two settings have to work around rather than inherit. Each appendix says how.

Fantasy is also the superset. Hedge Magic and Chartomancy are in this book; the Circles are one supplement away. A modern or science fiction game run on these rules will have something strange in it whether you plan for it or not — and if you'd rather it didn't, ignoring the magic aptitudes costs you nothing. Start here and subtract, rather than starting elsewhere and trying to add.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
Magic in the modern day. Run Appendix A for gear, occupations, and money. Add the Circle of Magic from Advanced Magic for characters who have it. Firearms and spellcasting already share a damage scale, so a pistol and a Conjure Flame sit in the same fight without anyone doing sums. The interesting question stops being does this balance and becomes who knows magic is real.

A traveller from elsewhere. The party is this book. One character is Appendix A or B — modern or far-future aptitudes, a sidearm with a hard ammunition limit, and gear nobody else can repair. The usage die is the whole story: every roll on that pistol brings them closer to being just another person in a strange place. Give them the Stranded keyword and let it earn advantage on knowing things and disadvantage on being trusted.

Post-apocalypse. Not an appendix at all — an assembly. Take Appendix A's gear and lethality, Appendix B's technology as ruins and salvage rather than equipment, and this book's foraging, travel, and light economy, which is the part that actually makes a wasteland feel like one. Scarcity comes free: run every consumable one usage die smaller than listed. A whole setting, and you wrote none of it.

Anything else. Weird West is this book's frontier travel with Appendix A's revolvers. Gaslamp horror is Appendix A held to this book's light rules. A generation ship is Appendix B with this book's exploration aptitudes, because a derelict deck is a dungeon. The seams are meant to be pulled at.

docs.title: One thing to watch
docs.text: Hold the line at d10 for weapon damage unless something is paying for the excess. The scale in Section 6 is what keeps a sword and a rifle in the same conversation; a weapon that quietly exceeds it takes the game over. Everything else — aptitudes, keywords, gear, money — mixes freely and needs no adjudication beyond a GM saying yes.

docs.title: Appendix A: Modern
docs.text:
Sirens, streetlights, and something in the storm drain. Roughly the present day — near enough that everyone at the table already knows how the world works.

Currency: prices use the same numbers as Section 6. A copper piece is a dollar; 1 sp is ten, 1 gp is a hundred. Call it whatever your setting calls it.

docs.text: Choose 2 at character creation, as normal.

docs.title: Skill Aptitudes
docs.text:
Occupations — what you did before this, or still do by day.

  • Detective: Advantage on tests to examine a scene, follow a paper trail, or read a suspect. Once per long rest, declare an intuition — the GM gives you one true fact about a current mystery
  • Medic: Stabilise a dying character with no test. Once per short rest, ten minutes of care restores 1d6 + WIS HP
  • Mechanic: Advantage on tests to repair, modify, or sabotage vehicles, electronics, and machinery. Identify the make and condition of unfamiliar equipment on an INT test DC 12
  • Soldier: No disadvantage with firearms. Advantage on tests to hold composure under fire or read a tactical situation
  • Researcher: Advantage on INT tests to recall academic knowledge in your field. Once per long rest, declare "I studied this" — the GM provides relevant background on a current topic
  • Journalist: Advantage on CHA tests to get information out of someone in an interview. Once per adventure, name a contact you know in your beat, and they exist
  • Engineer: Build or jury-rig a working device from what's on hand. INT test DC 12 and ten minutes for something simple — an alarm, a signal, a shaped charge, a weapon

Talents — competencies layered onto any character.

  • Driving: Advantage on DEX tests to handle a car, bike, or boat at speed
  • Firearms: No disadvantage with handguns, rifles, and shotguns. Quick Draw works with them
  • Computers: Advantage on INT tests to use, navigate, or break into computer systems. Recognise malware and basic intrusions on sight
  • Streetwise: Advantage to find black-market goods, locate criminal contacts, or read a neighbourhood's affiliations
  • Athletics: Advantage on STR/DEX tests for climbing, running, and moving through built environments at speed
  • Break and Enter: Advantage to defeat locks and alarms with tools. High-security systems roll normally. Without tools, at disadvantage
  • Move Silently and Unseen: Advantage to sneak, hide, and remain unnoticed
  • Silver Tongue: Advantage on CHA to negotiate, de-escalate, or convince — not against someone's core interests
  • Languages: Two additional languages. Can be taken more than once

docs.title: A5. Optional Rules
docs.text:
Lethal firearms. The list above keeps guns level with medieval weapons, which suits pulp and horror. For a game where a gunshot is a catastrophe, shift every firearm up one die and give non-ballistic armour no AC against them. Apply it to the enemies too — that's the whole point, and it makes a single hallway genuinely frightening.

Response time. Modern settings have police, ambulances, and fire crews. When something loud happens, roll a d6: that's how many rounds until sirens are audible. This one die does more to shape modern play than any equipment rule.

Paper trails. Everything modern characters do leaves a record — cameras, card transactions, phone location. Rather than tracking it, give the GM one Trace token each time the party is careless. Spent later, a Trace means someone found them.

docs.title: The information problem
docs.text:
This is the appendix's central difficulty and it needs solving at your table before session one.

Fantasy runs on a small information horizon: past a day's walk, everything is rumour, so the GM invents it and no one can check. Modern characters have a phone. Any mystery you improvise can be dissolved by a player who says "I look it up."

Don't ban the phone. Answer it. Pick whichever fits:

  • No signal. Basements, tunnels, storms, rural dead zones, deliberate jamming. Cheap, effective, and a reason to keep moving.
  • The record is wrong. The information exists and it's false — the file was altered, the obituary was printed for someone still alive. Now the search is the clue.
  • Access, not knowledge. They know the file exists. Getting it means a warrant, a favour, or a break-in. The obstacle moves from knowing to reaching.
  • It isn't written down. The thing they're chasing predates records, or is deliberately absent from them. A search that returns nothing is itself information.

The last one is the best of the four, and it's why modern horror works: the terrifying result is the empty one.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Modern Rath is not action-hero fiction by default. Characters have the same 10 + CON hit points as everyone else, which is two or three shots. The genre this system naturally produces is crime, investigation, and horror — people out of their depth in a world that mostly makes sense. Lean into that before you try to make it Die Hard.

Ordinary characters are the strength here. A nurse, a mechanic, and a reporter make a better party than three ex-special-forces operators, because the interesting question is what they're willing to do, not what they're able to.

And the world is documented, populated, and legible in a way a fantasy world isn't — which cuts both ways. Your players know how a hospital works, so you don't have to explain it. They also know what should happen when someone calls 911, which means the moment nobody comes is worth ten paragraphs of description.

docs.title: Appendix B: Science Fiction
docs.text:
Long distances, thin air, and salvage worth more than the ship. Anywhere from a grimy near-future to the far end of a long expansion.

Currency: prices use the same numbers as Section 6. A copper piece is a credit; 1 sp is ten, 1 gp is a hundred.

What changes: the aptitude list below replaces Step 1's, the keywords replace Step 2's suggestions, and the equipment replaces Section 6's. Sections 2 through 5 are unchanged.

docs.title: B1. Aptitudes
docs.text: Choose 2 at character creation, as normal.

docs.title: Skill Aptitudes
docs.text:
• Pilot: Advantage on DEX tests to fly, dock, or evade in any craft you've been checked out on. Once per long rest, attempt a manoeuvre the GM has called impossible
  • Void-Walker: Advantage on tests to work in vacuum, zero gravity, or a failing suit. You do not panic when the seal goes
  • Tech: Advantage on INT tests to repair, override, or sabotage machinery and software. Identify unfamiliar equipment's origin and condition on an INT test DC 12
  • Xenologist: Advantage on INT/WIS tests concerning non-human life, language, and artefacts. Once per long rest, declare one true thing about a creature or artefact you're examining
  • Corpsman: Stabilise a dying character with no test. Once per short rest, ten minutes of care restores 1d6 + WIS HP. Works on most non-human physiologies at disadvantage
  • Marine: No disadvantage with military weapons. Advantage on tests to hold formation, breach, or fight in low gravity
  • Salvager: Advantage to assess wreckage, find the valuable thing in a hold, or judge whether a structure is about to fail
  • Broker: Advantage on CHA to negotiate, appraise, or find a buyer. Once per adventure, name a contact at any station you've visited

Talents: Break and Enter, Move Silently and Unseen, Silver Tongue, Athletics, and Languages work as written in Appendix A.

Aptitude Reads as Darkvision / NightVision Ocular implant, or a species evolved somewhere dim Natural Armor Carapace, subdermal plating, a synthetic chassis Natural Weapons Claws, spurs, integrated tooling Tough Heavy-worlder, gene-modified, or simply built for it Small A low-gravity native, an engineered crew-form, a drone-body Wings Only meaningful in low gravity or with atmosphere — say which Hard to Pin Down Reflex modification

Two Skill Aptitudes means baseline human. One or more Inherent Aptitudes means you are something else — engineered, alien, augmented, or synthetic. Your keywords say which.

docs.title: B5. Optional Rules
docs.text:
Vacuum. No suit means a CON test DC 12 each round. Failure costs 1d6 HP and you're unconscious on the second failure. A holed suit runs its air on a UD6 instead of a UD8, and the sound of it is the best pressure a GM has.

Low and zero gravity. In low gravity, jumps and lifts get advantage and anything requiring traction gets disadvantage. In zero gravity, you move only by pushing off something — plan your route or drift. Void-Walker cancels the disadvantage.

Radiation and exposure. Treat as a condition per Section 5. Severity 4-6d6 depending on source, resisted with CON, and it doesn't stop when you leave the room.

Distance. Nothing kills a science fiction campaign faster than instant travel. Give every journey a duration in days and roll for one complication en route. A crew that can't simply leave is a crew with problems.

docs.title: The information problem
docs.text:
Science fiction has fantasy's problem in reverse: the characters have databases, sensors, and comms, and can in principle look up anything. Left alone, that dissolves improvised play the same way a phone does. The answers here are better than modern's, because the setting hands them to you:

  • Light-lag and distance. A query to the nearest archive takes hours or weeks. You will decide before the answer arrives.
  • The database is corporate. It contains what someone wanted in it. The redactions are the plot.
  • Nobody has been here. Survey and salvage games are built on the absence of records. The scanner tells you the mass and the temperature; it does not tell you what the thing is.
  • The sensors work fine. They report exactly what's there, and it makes no sense. This is the good one — trust the instruments and let the reading be the horror.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Keep it grubby. These rules give a starting character 10 + CON hit points and no shields, which means science fiction Rath is Alien and Firefly, not Star Wars. The ship needs repairs, the air is a resource, and nobody is coming.

Resist the technology arms race. The weapon list above tops out at the same d10 as a greatsword on purpose — the moment a plasma rifle does d12 because it sounds like it should, the fantasy appendix stops being playable at the same table and the whole structure of this book falls over. Make advanced technology interesting through traits and logistics, never through bigger numbers.

The strangeness in a science fiction game should be genuinely strange. A xeno that's just an orc with more arms wastes the setting. Ask what it wants, and make the answer something a human wouldn't want.

docs.title: Rath Freehand
docs.text: People in strange situations.

docs.title: What This Is
docs.text:
Rath Freehand is the whole of Rath in a dozen pages. Same dice, same stats, same maths — but no aptitude lists, no equipment catalogue, and nothing to read before you start.

You get a character in five minutes. You describe who they are in two or three words, and those words are the rules. A cop has a badge, a radio, and a pistol because of course she does — you don't look any of that up, you just write it down and start playing.

This is a GM-facing game. There is no table to consult when a player asks whether their character can do something. There is you, the fiction, and a d20. If that sounds like more work, it isn't — it's less. The rulebook stops being a thing you arbitrate against and becomes a thing you arbitrate with.

Use it for: one-shots, conventions, a setting you invented an hour ago, teaching someone their first RPG, a game where you don't yet know what genre you're in.

Use full Rath instead if: you want a long campaign with mechanical character growth, or your players like builds. Freehand deliberately gives up the build.

Compatible with everything. Freehand uses the same stats, the same DCs, the same damage scale, and the same injury table as the full game. You can run a published Rath adventure with Freehand characters, or drop a Freehand character into a full-Rath party, without converting anything.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
When the outcome is uncertain and failure costs something, roll:

d20 + stat ≥ 12

That's the whole resolution system. 12 is the target for almost everything.

  • Natural 20 — critical success. Something extra goes right.
  • Natural 1 — critical failure. Something goes wrong.

In a fight, you roll against the target's AC instead of 12.

Don't roll when you don't need to. If there's no real chance of failure, or failure isn't interesting, the character just does it.

docs.title: The Six Stats
docs.text:
Stat Used For STR Melee attacks, lifting, breaking, physical power DEX Ranged attacks, dodging, climbing, sneaking INT Knowledge, technical work, magic, crafting WIS Perception, tracking, navigation, noticing CON Toughness, resisting harm, healing CHA Persuasion, deception, intimidation, charm

Whichever stat best fits what the player described is the one they add. If two stats both fit, let them use the better one.

docs.title: The Advantage Scale
docs.text:
Every test sits somewhere on four steps:

Impossible → Disadvantage → Straight Roll → Advantage

Step Roll When Impossible No roll No training, no tools, or it simply can't be done Disadvantage 2d20, take lower Bad conditions, injured, working against your nature Straight Roll 1d20 The default Advantage 2d20, take higher A keyword applies, good tools, clever approach

Each factor moves you one step. Factors in the same direction don't stack — you can't get double advantage. Factors in opposite directions cancel one-for-one.

This scale is where keywords live. See Section 3.

docs.title: Fortune
docs.text:
Every character has Fortune, maximum 3. Start each session with 1. Gain 1 on a natural 20. The GM hands them out for good play.

Spend 1 Fortune to: - Reroll any test and keep the better result - Help an ally's roll, if you can describe how you're in position to - Declare something true that one of your keywords makes plausible (see Section 3)

docs.title: 2. Making a Character
docs.text: Five minutes, four steps, no lists.

docs.title: Step 1 — Say who they are
docs.text: One sentence. "A tired homicide detective three weeks from retirement." "A void-station welder who's never seen a planet." "The youngest daughter of a burned-out noble house."

docs.title: Step 2 — Pick 3 keywords
docs.text: Pull them out of the sentence. The detective is Police, Homicide Detective, Burned Out. See Section 3 for what makes a good one.

docs.title: Step 3 — Assign stats
docs.text:
Distribute 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0 across the six stats. Highest goes where the concept points.

Rolling instead: 3d6 per stat in order, take the lowest die of each. Then swap any two.

docs.title: Step 4 — Derive and equip
docs.text:
HP 10 + CON AC 10 + DEX + armour Slots 10 + CON

Then take whatever your keywords obviously imply, plus three things you name. The detective has a badge, a radio, cuffs, and a pistol without asking. Then she says: a photo of her daughter, a hip flask, and a lockpick set she isn't supposed to own.

The GM says yes, or says "not that, but you could have —". That's the entire equipment system. Section 4 covers the few things that need numbers.

Write it on an index card. Name, three keywords, six stats, HP, AC, what you're carrying, Fortune. That's a character sheet.

docs.title: 3. Keywords
docs.text:
Keywords are the only special-ability system in Freehand. Everything an aptitude, class, or feat would do in another game, a keyword does here.

A keyword is two or three words describing something true about your character. Not a stat, not a power — a fact. Police. Grew Up On The Docks. Wanted In Three Counties. Ex-Wyvern Rider. Very Large.

They do three things.

docs.title: They grant permission
docs.text:
This is the important one. A keyword can move a test from Impossible to a roll.

Without the Locksmith keyword, you don't get to attempt the vault's deadbolt — you have no idea what you're looking at. With it, you roll. Without Police, you can't talk your way past a crime-scene cordon at all; with it, you're arguing with a colleague.

This is what makes a character with four keywords different from one with two. Not a bigger bonus — a wider world of things they're allowed to try. Depth is capped. Breadth isn't.

docs.title: They grant advantage
docs.text:
When a keyword is clearly relevant to a roll you were already going to make, you get advantage. One step, once. A second applicable keyword adds nothing mechanically.

The player argues for it: "I'm a Homicide Detective — I've stood over a hundred bodies. I should have advantage reading this scene." The GM says yes or no. Say yes often.

docs.title: They let you declare
docs.text:
Spend 1 Fortune to declare a fact the world now contains, if one of your keywords makes it plausible.

"I'm Police. There's a patrol car parked on this block — there always is." "I Grew Up On The Docks. I know a way through the fence." "I'm Wanted In Three Counties. One of these guards has my face on a poster, and he's nervous about it."

The GM can narrow it, but shouldn't refuse it outright — if the keyword makes it plausible, the Fortune point has bought it. This is how a player writes the setting with you.

docs.title: What makes a good keyword
docs.text:
The test is how often it comes up.

Too broad Too narrow About right Adventurer Left-Handed Lockpicking Thief Skilled Allergic To Cats Ship's Doctor Strong Speaks Old High Vessin Raised By Wolves Good At Things Once Met The Duke Owes The Duke Money

Broad keywords apply to everything, so they stop meaning anything. Narrow ones never come up. Aim for something that'll matter two or three times a session.

Downsides count. Burned Out, Blind, Hunted, Terrible Liar are all excellent keywords. They grant permission and advantage in their own strange directions — being blind is an asset in the dark, being hunted means you know how the hunters think — and they earn Fortune when they cost you something. A keyword that only ever helps is a boring keyword.

docs.title: Keywords change
docs.text:
This is not a character sheet you fill in once.

Gain one when the story earns it. Survive a month in the marshes and you might take Marsh-Wise. Kill something famous and Dragonslayer is now true about you, for better and worse.

Lose one when the story takes it. Get struck off and Police is gone — though Ex-Police is a different and sometimes better keyword.

Swap one during any rest or scene break, if the fiction supports it.

Keep it to three active at a time. A character can be many things; three of them are load-bearing this session. Let players reshuffle which three between sessions.

GM: when a player invokes a keyword you don't think applies, don't say "no." Say "what does being Police have to do with this lock?" Half the time they have an answer you didn't think of, and it's better than the one you'd have given.

docs.title: 4. Gear
docs.text: There is no equipment list. There's a scale, and the GM prices things against it.

docs.title: Weapons
docs.text:
Pick a damage die. That's the weapon.

Damage Slots What it is d4 1 Improvised. A chair leg, a rock, a letter opener d6 1 Small or one-handed. Knife, club, pistol, hatchet d8 2 The standard. Sword, axe, rifle, spear d10 3 Heavy, or needs both hands. Greatsword, shotgun, poleaxe

Then take one trait free. Each extra trait costs +1 slot, or one step down the damage die.

Trait Effect Ranged (near) Attack to near distance, using DEX Ranged (far) Attack to far distance, using DEX Reload Action to reload after a few shots Piercing Ignores 2 AC Throwable Can be thrown to near Concealable Hidden under clothing, no test Quiet Doesn't give away your position Burst Two targets in near range, both at disadvantage

Worked example — a pistol. Start at d8 (a standard weapon, 2 slots). Ranged (near) is the free trait. Concealable costs one step down: d6, ranged, concealable, 2 slots. Want it to hit harder? Give up concealable and it's a d8. Want it in one slot? Drop to d4 or spend the slot elsewhere.

Worked example — a sniper rifle. d10, two-handed, 3 slots. Free trait: ranged (far). Add piercing and quiet — that's two extra traits, so either +2 slots (5 total, it's an enormous thing in a case) or step the damage down twice to d6 (a small, quiet, armour-piercing weapon that doesn't hit hard). Pick the one that matches the fiction.

d10 is the ceiling. Nothing a person picks up and uses does more than d10 without paying for it — a round spent aiming, an ammunition limit, a keyword requirement, or simple rarity. Break this and the weapon becomes the character.

docs.title: Armour
docs.text:
Armour AC Slots Notes Light +1 2 Leather, a padded coat, a concealed vest Medium +2 3 Mail, a flak jacket. Disadvantage on stealth Heavy +3 5 Plate, a hardsuit. Disadvantage on stealth and swimming Shield +1 1 Can be destroyed to absorb up to 15 damage Helmet +1 1

Whatever the setting calls it, it's one of these five.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Write it down. One slot each. You have 10 + CON slots.

Don't price it. Don't track coins unless money is what the game is about — and if it is, invent a unit and charge what feels right. Nobody has ever had a better session because the rope cost 1 silver.

docs.title: Things that run out
docs.text:
Ammunition, torches, rations, medical supplies, fuel — anything you'd rather not count. Give it a usage die and roll it when it's used:

d20 → d12 → d10 → d8 → d6 → d4 → gone

On a 1 or 2, the die shrinks one step. When a d4 comes up 1 or 2, you're out.

Roll ammunition once after each fight. Roll light sources every hour. Roll everything else when it'd be tense.

docs.title: Combat
docs.text:
Initiative: every round, each player rolls d20 + DEX vs 12. Success means they go before the enemies; failure means after. Reroll each round.

Order: players who passed → enemies → players who failed.

Faster: roll 1d6. On 1-3 the enemies go first, on 4-6 the players do.

Your turn: move up to near and take an action, or run up to far and do nothing else.

Attack: d20 + STR (melee) or DEX (ranged) vs the target's AC.

Damage: roll the weapon's die, add STR if it's melee. Max roll explodes — roll again and add, and keep going while you keep rolling max.

Natural 20: the target loses 1 AC for the rest of the fight. Natural 1: something goes wrong. GM decides what.

Two weapons: after your first attack, take a second at disadvantage. Stunts — shove, disarm, trip, grapple: opposed test, usually STR vs STR or DEX vs DEX. Reactions: one per round. Attack an enemy who leaves your reach, or throw yourself in front of an ally.

docs.title: Distance
docs.text: Range Roughly Close Arm's length. Melee Near Across a room. One move Far Across a street. A run Distant Further. Not part of this fight yet

docs.title: Getting hurt
docs.text:
At 0 HP: roll CON vs 12. Pass and you get 1d6 HP and stay up on adrenaline. Fail and you're down — you can crawl, nothing else, until the danger's over.

When the danger passes, roll 2d6:

2d6 2-3 Dead. Make the last words count 4-6 Maimed. Something permanent. +1d6 HP 7-9 Broken. A week off your feet. +1d6 HP 10-11 Battered. A day. +1d6 HP 12 Tough bastard. +2d6 HP, back on your feet

A maiming is a new keyword. One Eye. Bad Leg. Ruined Hand. Write it down.

docs.title: Resting
docs.text: Short rest — an hour somewhere reasonably safe: recover 1d6 + CON HP. Long rest — a night somewhere actually safe: back to full.

docs.title: Getting better
docs.text:
Freehand has no levels by default. Characters change by gaining and losing keywords, and that's usually enough — a one-shot doesn't need an XP economy.

If you're running it longer and want progression, use this and nothing else:

After each session, one of: raise a stat by 1 (max 6), or take a fourth keyword slot (max 5 total). That's it. Roll 1d6 and add it to your max HP every third session if the players want to feel sturdier.

docs.title: 6. Dials
docs.text:
Set these before session one. Say them out loud so the table agrees.

Lethality. The default is dangerous — a d8 to the chest is a third of a starting character. To go deadlier, drop starting HP to 5 + CON. To go pulpier, let players spend Fortune to negate a hit entirely.

Guns. The scale above treats a pistol as a d6 and a rifle as a d8, which puts them level with a knife and a sword. That looks wrong at first — surely a rifle beats a longbow — but damage isn't where firearms win. They win on traits: a bow spends its one free trait just getting to far range, while a rifle gets there and can still afford piercing (armour was built for arrows, not bullets), burst, or quiet with a suppressor. Two weapons, the same die, and the gun is doing three things the bow can't. That's the distinction, and the scale already carries it.

If you want firearms frightening on top of that, shift every gun up one die and give non-ballistic armour no AC against them. Apply it to the enemies too — that's the whole point.

Grit. For survival games, start every consumable one usage die lower than you otherwise would, and require a ration on any day of hard travel.

Magic and the strange. There are no spell lists here. If a character is a wizard, Wizard is their keyword: it grants permission to attempt magical things and advantage when doing them, and the roll is INT vs 12. Failure should cost something — describe what. If you want an actual magic system, that's what full Rath's Advanced Magic is for, and it drops straight in.

Session zero in one question. Ask each player: "what's the worst thing that could plausibly happen to your character?" Write the answers down. That's your adventure.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Test: d20 + stat ≥ 12. Nat 20 crit, nat 1 fumble. Attack: d20 + STR/DEX ≥ AC. Damage explodes on max. Advantage: Impossible → Disadvantage → Straight → Advantage. One step per factor, no stacking, opposites cancel. Keywords: 3 active. Grant permission, grant advantage, and — for 1 Fortune — let you declare a fact. Fortune: max 3. Reroll, help an ally, or declare. Start each session with 1, gain on a nat 20. Weapons: d4/d6 = 1 slot, d8 = 2, d10 = 3. One trait free, extras cost a slot or a die step. d10 is the ceiling. Armour: Light +1 / Medium +2 / Heavy +3 / Shield +1 / Helmet +1. Carrying: 10 + CON slots. One slot per item unless it's obviously bigger. HP: 10 + CON. AC: 10 + DEX + armour. At 0 HP: CON vs 12 to stay up. Then 2d6 on the injury table. Rest: short = 1d6 + CON. Long = full. Usage die: d20 → d12 → d10 → d8 → d6 → d4 → gone. Shrinks on a 1-2.

docs.title: Rath Overdrive
docs.text:
The Rider expansion for Rath RPG. Empowered champions, modular gear-driven transformations, and the dramatic buildup arcs of tokusatsu hero fiction.

A Rider is a person bonded to a transformation device — a Driver — that grants them dramatically enhanced ability for short windows. While transformed (in Henshin), a Rider is a focused and dangerous combatant whose power is themed by the Inserts loaded into their Driver.

Riders are not mages. They do not cast spells. Their power lives in their gear, and in the momentum of the fight itself.

Everything a Rider tracks: one number (Charge), the Inserts in their Driver, and how many transformations they have left today. That's it — it fits on a normal character sheet.

Setting: Rath Overdrive assumes a modern-day game. Use Appendix A of the Players Handbook for occupations, gear, and tone; this book adds only the Rider layer on top. It reflavours cleanly into any setting as a "blessed champion" archetype with GM approval.

docs.title: 1. Becoming a Rider
docs.text:
There are two ways in.

Start as one. Take Henshin at character creation, where it costs both of your starting aptitudes. You begin play already bonded to a Driver, already able to transform — and with nothing else. Everything you can do that an ordinary person can't comes out of the belt. That's the trade, and it's the right one for a campaign that opens with the Driver already on your hip.

Because two slots buy what one otherwise would, a creation Rider tops out one aptitude short of everyone else. In exchange, you have been doing this long enough that it comes easily: you transform with 1 additional Charge — 4 instead of 3, or 6 instead of 5 with Reinforced Core.

Become one. Take Henshin as an Advanced Aptitude at level 3, 5, 7, or 9, the normal way. Your character was someone before they were a Rider, and they keep being that person underneath. Finding the Driver is a story you get to play through rather than one you write in your backstory.

Either way, the rest of the tree is Advanced Aptitudes taken at 3, 5, 7, or 9 as usual. A specialist can take all four.

  • Henshin (required entry) — You are bonded to a Driver. As an action, transform. You may Henshin L times per long rest. While transformed you have +2 AC and advantage on tests to resist fear, intimidation, and mental influence. You transform at 3 Charge, your Charge cap is 6, and your Driver has 1 Insert slot.

  • Expanded Driver (requires Henshin) — Your Driver gains +1 Insert slot. May be taken twice, to a maximum of three slots.

  • Reinforced Core (requires Henshin) — Your Charge cap rises to 8, and you transform at 5 Charge instead of 3.

  • Finisher Mastery (requires Henshin) — Your Finisher deals +1d6, and immediately after using one you gain 1 Charge. Spent everything? The Driver gives you just enough back to still be standing.

Multiclassing: apart from the creation option above, Henshin uses Advanced Aptitude slots like any other path. A Rider can also be a Hedge Mage, Chartomancer, or Circle Mage, but four slots across two paths spreads thin. Pure Riders specialise.

Starting at level 1. A Rider who begins play as one is powerful in a way no other level 1 character is — but narrowly. L is 1, so you get one transformation per day; you have no other aptitudes at all; and while you start each Henshin at 4 Charge, your opening Finisher is only 5d6. Reaching the big numbers still takes rounds of fighting, and out of Henshin you are an ordinary person with a belt. If it feels too strong at your table, the dial is the same as always: drop the Finisher to (Charge spent)d6.

docs.title: 2. Charge
docs.text:
Charge is the whole system. One number, from 0 to your cap. It only exists while you are transformed, and it does four jobs at once:

Charge is… Which means Fuel for your Inserts Spending makes you fragile Fuel for your Finisher Spending it all leaves you one hit from powering down Your transformation's timer At 0, the next hit ends it Your buffer against anti-Rider attacks Getting hit refuels you and threatens you

Because of the last two, a Rider who disengages loses their transformation. You cannot kite, hide, or wait it out. You have to stay in the fight.

docs.title: Building Charge
docs.text:
Trigger Charge Strike — attack normally, hit or miss +1 Charge up — attack, and forgo all damage from it +2 You are hit by an attack, or take a hit for an ally via Protect +1 The GM awards a cinematic beat — a rival's challenge answered, a civilian saved, a named attack called out +1 (once or twice a scene)

You cannot exceed your cap. Charge does not carry between transformations.

This is the trade. A Rider who wants a huge Finisher has to spend rounds dealing no damage to get there. Burst is bought with sustain, at a fixed rate, and it balances itself — you do not need to adjudicate it.

docs.title: Spending Charge
docs.text: Charge pays for Inserts (Section 5) and the Finisher (Section 4). Both are optional; a Rider who spends nothing simply fights on with +2 AC and a full pool.

docs.title: Losing Charge
docs.text:
Ordinary attacks damage HP as normal. Some enemies carry anti-Rider attacks that strip Charge instead (Section 6).

At 0 Charge you are still transformed — but barely. This is a Rider's last stand:

  • You keep your +2 AC and everything else Henshin gives you
  • You no longer gain Charge from being hit
  • You do still gain Charge from striking, charging up, and cinematic beats — land a blow and you're back in the fight
  • Any damage you take ends the transformation. You take the damage as normal to HP, and you are forced out

Spending your pool does not detransform you. Only taking a hit at 0 does.

docs.title: 3. Henshin and Detransformation
docs.text:
Transforming is an action. It never fails while you hold your Driver — there is no roll.

You drop out of Henshin in one of three ways:

Trigger Effect Voluntary Free action, any time. Charge is lost Damage taken while at 0 Charge Forced out. The damage applies to HP as normal. You are dazed for one round — you may move, but take no actions HP reduced to 0 Forced out, and you enter Rath's at-0-HP rules as normal (CON test DC 12)

Re-transforming costs another use of Henshin. With none left, you are done for the day.

Without your Driver you cannot Henshin. Taking a Rider's Driver is a story beat, never a routine combat action — it needs real setup, an opportunity such as a grapple or an ambush, and an opposed test at major disadvantage. Destroying one is a campaign event, not a tactical outcome.

docs.title: 4. The Finisher
docs.text:
Every Rider has one, whatever their Inserts. Name it at the table.

Finisher — Action. Spend any amount of Charge. Deal (Charge spent + 1)d6 damage to one target in near range.

Spend 3, deal 4d6. Spend 6, deal 7d6.

Emptying your pool does not power you down — but it leaves you at 0 Charge, where the next hit that lands ends the transformation. That's the decision the Finisher really asks: cash out everything for the biggest number and finish the fight now, or hold a point back and stay in it.

A Rider standing at 0 Charge, everything spent, still swinging, is the shot the whole genre is built around. Let it happen.

docs.title: 5. Inserts
docs.text:
Inserts are the modular engines that define what kind of Rider you are. Flavour them however your table likes — Memories, Cards, Coins, Crystals, Discs, Rings. The mechanics are identical.

An Insert is one effect with one Charge cost. Treat it like a spell you happen to keep in your pocket.

Acquisition is narrative and GM-controlled. Inserts are found, awarded, inherited, salvaged from a defeated rival, or built by an ally who knows how. You do not buy them and you do not design them unilaterally — a new Insert is a conversation between player and GM at the moment it enters play, which is where its effect and cost get agreed. A Rider who wants a specific Insert should go and earn it; that's an adventure.

Inserts live in your inventory and take no slots — they're the size of a coin. Only the ones loaded into your Driver can be used. Loading or swapping an Insert takes a minute of downtime; you cannot do it mid-fight.

You start with one Insert of your choosing, agreed with the GM at character creation.

docs.title: The Cost Ladder
docs.text:
This is the reference for negotiating a new Insert. It's the Rider equivalent of spell levels — an Insert should do roughly what its cost says it does.

Charge Combat effect 1 One target, minor. +1d6 on a hit; +2 AC for a round; a free reposition; a reaction that negates one attack against you 2 Area or control. 2d6 in a cone or burst; a save-or-lose-your-turn; a move-and-attack combination 3 Heavy. 3d6 in a burst; or solid damage plus a lasting condition; or a strong single-target effect Charge Utility effect 1 Advantage on one test. If the Insert's theme plausibly covers it, this can also move a test from Impossible to a roll — the suit lets you attempt something you simply couldn't 2 Treat the relevant stat as 6 for one test 3 Succeed automatically at something a roll could have achieved

An Insert may carry a combat effect, a utility effect, or one of each — but each is bought separately at its own cost.

Utility Inserts are not free. You cannot build Charge outside a fight: no attacks, no hits, no cinematic beats. Whatever you spend out of combat is gone, and you walk into the next fight short. Transforming purely to solve a problem also burns one of your daily transformations. Lifting a fallen girder off a trapped civilian should feel like it cost you something, because it did.

docs.title: Losing Inserts
docs.text: An Insert loaded in a Driver can be knocked free by a called shot at −2. It lands within close range, inert until retrieved and reloaded — which takes a minute, so it's out for that fight. Inserts carried in inventory can't be targeted in combat, but can be stolen, lost, or destroyed in the fiction. Destroyed Inserts are gone; new ones come through play.

docs.title: 6. Anti-Rider Threats
docs.text:
Most enemies are ordinary HP threats and a transformed Rider will carve through them. That is correct — a Rider should feel powerful against a monster of the week.

The dangerous ones carry anti-Rider attacks, which strip Charge instead of HP. These make a Rider's own resource into their health bar, and they are the only thing that reliably ends a transformation early.

Keep the numbers small — the pool is only 0–8.

Threat Anti-Rider attack Kaijin disruptor On a hit: 1d4 Charge, no HP damage Anti-Rider weapon On a hit: normal HP damage and 1 Charge Draining aura 1 Charge at the start of each turn spent in near range Rival Rider's Finisher 1d6 Charge, and any excess spills to HP as normal

Use them sparingly. A session where every enemy strips Charge is a session where nobody gets to be a Rider.

GM: anti-Rider attacks are how you make the rival, the counter-built kaijin, and the Big Bad feel different from the week's monster — not by giving them more HP, but by threatening the thing the player actually cares about.

docs.title: 7. Sample Inserts
docs.text:
Four Inserts as calibration. Use them as written, or as a yardstick when a player brings you a new one.

Crimson Blaze — Fire / Aggression

The gear runs hot, leaving scorch lines where the Rider stands. - Combat (2 Charge): All creatures in a near cone make a DEX test DC 12. Failure takes 2d6 fire, success takes half. - Utility (1 Charge): Advantage on any test to burn, melt, weld, or endure heat.

Verdict — Speed / Mobility

Harder to pin than to hit, and harder to hit than to predict. - Combat (1 Charge): Reaction when an attack targets you — that attack misses. Once per round. - Utility (2 Charge): Treat your DEX as 6 for one test.

Verdant Bulwark — Nature / Endurance

The plating thickens and roots. Movement slows; presence becomes immovable. - Combat (1 Charge): Until you move from this spot, +2 AC and immunity to forced movement and knockdown. - Utility (2 Charge): Treat your STR as 6 for one test.

Cogitator — Tech / Cognition

The visor fills with cascading readouts. The Rider stops being a person for a moment and starts being a process. - Utility (1 Charge): Advantage on an INT test. If the problem is one you had no way to approach — an encrypted archive, an unknown script, a machine you've never seen — this lets you attempt it at all. - Utility (3 Charge): Automatically succeed at retrieving a specific piece of information that exists in a system you can reach.

Cogitator carries no combat effect, and that is a legitimate Insert. A Rider who loads it is trading a fight option for the ability to crack the case — and in a modern game, cracking the case is usually the adventure.

docs.title: 8. Notes on Balance
docs.text:
Riders should feel powerful and be spending for it. Measured against a level 5 character with a d8 weapon and STR 3 — roughly 7 or 8 damage a round:

Fight length Fighter Rider 4 rounds (strike, strike, Insert, Finish for 5) ~30 ~43 7 rounds (two Finishers, three charge-up rounds) ~52 ~60

Ahead at both lengths, and by a similar margin — that consistency is deliberate. It costs two or three Advanced Aptitude slots, and Henshin is limited to L uses a day.

Note what the charge-up rounds do to the average: a Rider who Finishes twice across seven rounds still only manages about 8.6 damage a round against a fighter's 7.5, because reaching those Finishers meant three rounds of dealing nothing at all. The exchange rate is the balance. For comparison, a Circle Mage's Arcane Blast at that level is around 20 damage for a single burn, several times a day.

Three things keep it honest, and you should not remove any of them:

  1. Charge-up costs damage. Reaching a big Finisher means rounds of dealing nothing. The exchange rate does the balancing so you don't have to.
  2. Charge is the health bar. Every point spent is a point of buffer gone, and at 0 the next hit ends you. A Rider who spends freely is a Rider one blow from being a civilian.
  3. You start at 3. A Rider cannot open with their best move — the biggest turn-one Finisher is 4d6, and anything more has to be earned in the fight.

If Riders feel too strong at your table, the first dial is the Finisher: try (Charge spent)d6 instead of (Charge + 1)d6 before touching anything else. If they feel too weak, raise the cinematic-beat award to twice a scene reliably — it's the cheapest lever and it rewards the play you want.

Do not hand out Inserts above 3 Charge, and do not let an Insert replicate the Finisher at a lower cost. Those are the two failure modes.

For modern-day occupations, gear, and tone, see Appendix A of the Rath RPG Players Handbook. For advanced aptitudes generally, see Advanced Aptitudes. For the magic paths a Rider might also walk, see Advanced Magic.

docs.title: Science Fiction
docs.text:
This is Appendix B of the Players Handbook. The core rules — tests, combat, character creation — are the same for every setting; only the aptitudes, keywords, and equipment change.

See Mixing Settings for running more than one at the same table.

Long distances, thin air, and salvage worth more than the ship. Anywhere from a grimy near-future to the far end of a long expansion.

Currency: prices use the same numbers as Section 6. A copper piece is a credit; 1 sp is ten, 1 gp is a hundred.

What changes: the aptitude list below replaces Step 1's, the keywords replace Step 2's suggestions, and the equipment replaces Section 6's. Sections 2 through 5 are unchanged.

docs.title: B1. Aptitudes
docs.text: Choose 2 at character creation, as normal.

docs.title: Skill Aptitudes
docs.text:
• Pilot: Advantage on DEX tests to fly, dock, or evade in any craft you've been checked out on. Once per long rest, attempt a manoeuvre the GM has called impossible
  • Void-Walker: Advantage on tests to work in vacuum, zero gravity, or a failing suit. You do not panic when the seal goes
  • Tech: Advantage on INT tests to repair, override, or sabotage machinery and software. Identify unfamiliar equipment's origin and condition on an INT test DC 12
  • Xenologist: Advantage on INT/WIS tests concerning non-human life, language, and artefacts. Once per long rest, declare one true thing about a creature or artefact you're examining
  • Corpsman: Stabilise a dying character with no test. Once per short rest, ten minutes of care restores 1d6 + WIS HP. Works on most non-human physiologies at disadvantage
  • Marine: No disadvantage with military weapons. Advantage on tests to hold formation, breach, or fight in low gravity
  • Salvager: Advantage to assess wreckage, find the valuable thing in a hold, or judge whether a structure is about to fail
  • Broker: Advantage on CHA to negotiate, appraise, or find a buyer. Once per adventure, name a contact at any station you've visited

Talents: Break and Enter, Move Silently and Unseen, Silver Tongue, Athletics, and Languages work as written in Appendix A.

docs.title: Inherent Aptitudes
docs.text:
Use Section 4's Inherent Aptitudes, read differently:

Aptitude Reads as Darkvision / NightVision Ocular implant, or a species evolved somewhere dim Natural Armor Carapace, subdermal plating, a synthetic chassis Natural Weapons Claws, spurs, integrated tooling Tough Heavy-worlder, gene-modified, or simply built for it Small A low-gravity native, an engineered crew-form, a drone-body Wings Only meaningful in low gravity or with atmosphere — say which Hard to Pin Down Reflex modification

Two Skill Aptitudes means baseline human. One or more Inherent Aptitudes means you are something else — engineered, alien, augmented, or synthetic. Your keywords say which.

docs.text:

docs.title: B5. Optional Rules
docs.text:
Vacuum. No suit means a CON test DC 12 each round. Failure costs 1d6 HP and you're unconscious on the second failure. A holed suit runs its air on a UD6 instead of a UD8, and the sound of it is the best pressure a GM has.

Low and zero gravity. In low gravity, jumps and lifts get advantage and anything requiring traction gets disadvantage. In zero gravity, you move only by pushing off something — plan your route or drift. Void-Walker cancels the disadvantage.

Radiation and exposure. Treat as a condition per Section 5. Severity 4-6d6 depending on source, resisted with CON, and it doesn't stop when you leave the room.

Distance. Nothing kills a science fiction campaign faster than instant travel. Give every journey a duration in days and roll for one complication en route. A crew that can't simply leave is a crew with problems.

docs.title: The information problem
docs.text:
Science fiction has fantasy's problem in reverse: the characters have databases, sensors, and comms, and can in principle look up anything. Left alone, that dissolves improvised play the same way a phone does. The answers here are better than modern's, because the setting hands them to you:

  • Light-lag and distance. A query to the nearest archive takes hours or weeks. You will decide before the answer arrives.
  • The database is corporate. It contains what someone wanted in it. The redactions are the plot.
  • Nobody has been here. Survey and salvage games are built on the absence of records. The scanner tells you the mass and the temperature; it does not tell you what the thing is.
  • The sensors work fine. They report exactly what's there, and it makes no sense. This is the good one — trust the instruments and let the reading be the horror.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Keep it grubby. These rules give a starting character 10 + CON hit points and no shields, which means science fiction Rath is Alien and Firefly, not Star Wars. The ship needs repairs, the air is a resource, and nobody is coming.

Resist the technology arms race. The weapon list above tops out at the same d10 as a greatsword on purpose — the moment a plasma rifle does d12 because it sounds like it should, the fantasy appendix stops being playable at the same table and the whole structure of this book falls over. Make advanced technology interesting through traits and logistics, never through bigger numbers.

The strangeness in a science fiction game should be genuinely strange. A xeno that's just an orc with more arms wastes the setting. Ask what it wants, and make the answer something a human wouldn't want.
